The Book of Mormon. A sacred text of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, purportedly translated by Joseph Smith in 1829 from golden plates he claimed to discover. It describes the history of ancient peoples in the Americas and presents Christianity as continuing revelation beyond the Bible.

Joseph Smith stated that an angel named Moroni revealed the location of golden plates inscribed with a history of pre-Columbian American peoples. The text describes Nephite and Lamanite civilizations spanning from around 600 BCE to 421 CE, with Jesus Christ appearing to them after his resurrection. This narrative of Christ's appearance to ancient American peoples is central to the Book of Mormon.

The text is organized into 15 books—Nephi, Jacob, Enos, and others—each further subdivided into chapters and verses, closely mimicking biblical structure. The central narrative describes the struggle between the Nephites, portrayed as righteous, and the Lamanites, portrayed as fallen. Over centuries this conflict escalates until the Lamanites ultimately destroy the Nephites. According to the text, the Lamanites became ancestors of Native Americans.

The Book of Mormon emphasizes continuing revelation, rejecting the sufficiency of the Bible alone. Jesus is presented as the central figure of all scriptural periods. Joseph Smith's translation methods remain debated. He reported using a seer stone and the golden plates, which he said were returned to the angel Moroni. The text fundamentally shaped LDS theology, including doctrines of premortal existence, eternal families, and temple ceremonies. The Book of Mormon claims continuity with biblical Christianity while asserting additional revelation through Joseph Smith as the founder and translator who brought the text forth.
